title: Project: Data dashboard CLI
subtitle: Load, clean, analyse and report, from the command line
goal: Build a command-line sales dashboard that cleans a messy CSV, computes KPIs, ranks products, prints ASCII charts and takes argparse filters.
outcomes: Profile a raw CSV export and plan a data pipeline as small functions
Clean, dedupe and aggregate real sales data into KPIs
Rank products and print a formatted report with ASCII bar charts
Compute the same KPIs with a SQL GROUP BY
Add command-line filters with argparse and test them with parse_args

slides.title: Mission 50: Project, a data dashboard CLI
slides.body:
Phase 5 finale. You'll build a command-line **sales dashboard**: load a messy CSV, clean it, compute KPIs, rank products and print a report with ASCII charts, then add filters with `argparse`.

First, a quick review of the phase.

items: Report with bars, plus CLI filters

slides.say: Welcome to the phase five finale. Today you build a real tool: a command line sales dashboard. It loads a messy CSV export, cleans it, computes the key numbers by month and by region, ranks the best products, prints a report with text charts, and takes command line filters with argparse. First, a quick review of the phase.

slides.title: Review: Big-O
slides.q: A function loops over n orders and, for each one, checks `if order_id in seen_list`. What's its Big-O, and the fix?
options: O(log n): sort the list first
slides.why: `in` on a list is a hidden O(n) loop, inside an O(n) loop: O(n²). A set makes each check O(1), so the whole function becomes O(n). (Day 41)
slides.say: Review time, starting with day forty one. This function loops over n orders and checks each order ID against a list of ones already seen. What is its Big O, and how do you fix it?

slides.title: Review: pick the algorithm
slides.q: Only one of these pairings is right. Which?
options: Fewest coins: always grab the biggest coin first
Find an ID in a sorted list of 1 million: binary search, about 20 checks
slides.why: Binary search halves a sorted list each step: about 20 checks for a million items (Day 42). Fewest stops needs BFS (Day 44), and greedy coin change fails for coins like 1, 3, 4: use dynamic programming.
slides.say: Days forty two to forty four. Only one of these pairings of problem and algorithm is right. Which one?

slides.title: Review: heaps
slides.code:
import heapq
tasks = []
for priority, name in [(2, "email"), (1, "deploy"), (3, "lunch"), (1, "backup")]:
    heapq.heappush(tasks, (priority, name))
print([heapq.heappop(tasks)[1] for _ in range(3)])
slides.why: `heappop` always returns the smallest tuple. The two priority-1 tasks tie, so their names decide: 'backup' < 'deploy'. That's why Day 43's scheduler added a counter, to break ties by arrival instead.
slides.say: Day forty three: a heap of tasks, and two of them share priority one. Which three task names come out first?

slides.title: Review: the web and databases
slides.q: Which line is a serious security bug?
slides.why: Pasting user input into SQL with an f-string allows SQL injection (Day 48). Placeholders, urlencode and timeouts are all good habits from Days 46 to 48.
slides.say: Days forty six to forty eight. One of these lines is a serious security bug. Spot it.

slides.title: Review: async
slides.q: `await asyncio.gather(fetch('a'), fetch('b'), fetch('c'))`: in what order do the results come back?
options: In the order the calls finish
In the order you passed them: a, b, c
slides.why: `gather` runs everything concurrently but always returns results in argument order, even if `c` finishes first. (Day 49)
slides.say: And day forty nine. Gather runs three fetches at once. In what order do the results come back?

slides.title: Design before you code
slides.body: Plan the dashboard as **small functions with clear inputs and outputs**. Each is easy to test on its own; `report` just glues them together.
slides.say: Before writing any code, design the pipeline as small functions with clear inputs and outputs. Load sales returns clean rows and a dropped count. Revenue by groups by any column. Top products ranks. Bar lines draws. Report just glues them together. Each piece can be tested on its own, which is exactly how professionals build tools.

slides.title: One grouping function for every KPI
slides.code:
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict

rows = [
    {"month": "2026-01", "region": "North", "product": "Earbuds", "revenue": 4497.0},
    {"month": "2026-01", "region": "South", "product": "Power bank", "revenue": 2598.0},
    {"month": "2026-02", "region": "North", "product": "Smartwatch", "revenue": 9998.0},
    {"month": "2026-02", "region": "West", "product": "Earbuds", "revenue": 2998.0},
]

def revenue_by(rows, key):
    totals = defaultdict(float)
    for row in rows:
        totals[row[key]] += row["revenue"]
    return dict(totals)

print(revenue_by(rows, "month"))
print(revenue_by(rows, "region"))
print(heapq.nlargest(2, revenue_by(rows, "product").items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]))
explain: key is the column to group by: 'month', 'region' or 'product'.
row[key] picks the group for this row.
nlargest: top-k from Day 43, no full sort needed.
slides.say: Here is the key design idea, on four clean rows. Instead of writing one function per report, revenue by takes the column name as a parameter, so the same five lines give revenue by month, by region or by product. Then heapq's n largest, from day forty three, picks the best sellers without sorting everything.

slides.title: Text bars for the report
slides.code:
def bar_lines(data, width=20):
    top = max(data.values(), default=0) or 1
    pad = max((len(label) for label in data), default=0)
    return [f"{label:<{pad}} {'█' * round(value / top * width)} ₹{value:,.0f}"
            for label, value in data.items()]

by_month = {"2026-01": 19783.0, "2026-02": 29282.0, "2026-03": 36581.0}
print("Revenue by month")
for line in bar_lines(by_month):
    print("  " + line)

jan, mar = by_month["2026-01"], by_month["2026-03"]
print(f"Q1 growth, January to March: {(mar - jan) / jan:.0%}")
explain: default=0 handles an empty dict; or 1 avoids dividing by zero.
Pad every label to the longest one.
Scale each value to blocks and format the money.
slides.say: This is the bar chart helper from day forty five, tightened up. Default equals zero lets max work on an empty dict, and or one avoids dividing by zero. The real monthly numbers from our data show steady growth, and the percent format spec turns a ratio into a percentage for us.

slides.title: The same KPIs in SQL
slides.code:
import csv, sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE sales (order_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, month TEXT, region TEXT, revenue REAL)")
with open("sales.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for r in csv.DictReader(f):
        units, price = r["units"].strip(), r["unit_price"].replace("₹", "").strip()
        if units.isdigit():
            conn.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO sales VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
                         (r["order_id"], r["date"][:7], r["region"].strip().title(), int(units) * float(price)))

for region, revenue, orders in conn.execute("""
        SELECT region, SUM(revenue), COUNT(*) FROM sales
        GROUP BY region ORDER BY SUM(revenue) DESC"""):
    print(f"{region:<6} ₹{revenue:>7,.0f}  ({orders} orders)")

slides.title: Project: the sales dashboard

The tests check each function.

slides.solution:
import csv
from collections import defaultdict

def parse_number(text):
    """'₹1,299' -> 1299.0; blank or junk -> None"""
    cleaned = text.replace("₹", "").replace(",", "").strip()
    try:
        return float(cleaned)
    except ValueError:
        return None

def bar_lines(data, width=20):
    """{label: value} -> aligned text bars (from Day 45)"""
    top = max(data.values(), default=0) or 1
    pad = max((len(label) for label in data), default=0)
    return [f"{label:<{pad}} {'█' * round(value / top * width)} ₹{value:,.0f}"
            for label, value in data.items()]

def load_sales(path):
    """Return (rows, dropped). Skip bad numbers and repeated order_ids."""
    rows, seen, dropped = [], set(), 0
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for raw in csv.DictReader(f):
            units, price = parse_number(raw["units"]), parse_number(raw["unit_price"])
            if raw["order_id"] in seen or units is None or price is None:
                dropped += 1
                continue
            seen.add(raw["order_id"])
            rows.append({
                "order_id": raw["order_id"],
                "month": raw["date"][:7],
                "region": raw["region"].strip().title(),
                "product": raw["product"].strip(),
                "units": int(units),
                "revenue": units * price,
            })
    return rows, dropped

def revenue_by(rows, key):
    """Total revenue for each value of row[key]."""
    totals = defaultdict(float)
    for row in rows:
        totals[row[key]] += row["revenue"]
    return dict(totals)

def top_products(rows, n=3):
    """[(product, revenue), ...] for the n best sellers, biggest first."""
    totals = revenue_by(rows, "product")
    return sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)[:n]

def report(rows, dropped):
    print("SALES DASHBOARD · Q1 2026")
    print(f"Orders: {len(rows)} (dropped {dropped} bad rows)")
    total = sum(r["revenue"] for r in rows)
    print(f"Total revenue: ₹{total:,.0f}")
    print(f"Average order: ₹{total / len(rows):,.0f}" if rows else "Average order: n/a")
    print()
    print("Revenue by month")
    for line in bar_lines(dict(sorted(revenue_by(rows, "month").items()))):
        print("  " + line)
    print()
    print("Revenue by region")
    by_region = sorted(revenue_by(rows, "region").items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)
    for line in bar_lines(dict(by_region)):
        print("  " + line)
    print()
    print("Top 3 products")
    for rank, (product, revenue) in enumerate(top_products(rows), 1):
        print(f"  {rank}. {product:<11} ₹{revenue:,.0f}")

rows, dropped = load_sales("sales.csv")
report(rows, dropped)
slides.tests:
rows, dropped = load_sales("sales.csv")
assert dropped == 3, f"sales.csv has 2 rows with bad units and 1 duplicate order, so dropped should be 3, not {dropped}."
assert len(rows) == 19, f"19 clean orders should remain, not {len(rows)}."
regions = sorted({r["region"] for r in rows})
assert regions == ["East", "North", "South", "West"], f"Each region needs one spelling (strip, then title-case). Got {regions}."
s9 = [r for r in rows if r["order_id"] == "S009"]
assert len(s9) == 1 and s9[0]["revenue"] == 3897.0, "S009 is 3 power banks at ₹1299 (strip the ₹): revenue 3897.0, kept only once."
assert rows[0]["month"] == "2026-01" and isinstance(rows[0]["units"], int), "Each row needs a month like '2026-01' (date[:7]) and units as an int."
by_month = revenue_by(rows, "month")
assert by_month == {"2026-01": 19783.0, "2026-02": 29282.0, "2026-03": 36581.0}, f"Revenue by month should be Jan 19783, Feb 29282, Mar 36581. Got {by_month}."
by_region = revenue_by(rows, "region")
assert by_region.get("South") == 28088.0 and by_region.get("West") == 11788.0, f"South should total 28088 and West 11788. Got {by_region}."
assert revenue_by([], "region") == {}, "revenue_by on no rows should return an empty dict."
top = top_products(rows)
assert [p for p, _ in top] == ["Smartwatch", "Earbuds", "Power bank"], f"The top 3 products are Smartwatch, Earbuds and Power bank. Got {top}."
assert top[0][1] == 39992.0, "Smartwatch revenue should be 39992.0."
assert len(top_products(rows, 5)) == 5 and top_products(rows, 1) == top[:1], "top_products should return exactly n products."
assert "85,646" in __out__, "The report should print the total revenue, ₹85,646 (format it with :,.0f)."
assert "Smartwatch" in __out__ and "█" in __out__, "The report should show the ASCII bars and the top products."
hints: Day 45's pattern: parse units and price with `parse_number`; if either is None, or the id is already in `seen`, add 1 to `dropped` and `continue`.

slides.title: argparse: options for your tool
slides.body:
`argparse` turns `--region West --top 5` into `args.region == 'West'` and `args.top == 5`, and writes `--help` for free. You'll go deeper on Day 51.

In tests, pass a list: `parser.parse_args(['--top', '5'])`. On bad input, argparse prints an error and **exits**.
slides.say: Argparse turns command line text, like dash dash region West, into a tidy object where args dot region is West and args dot top is five. It even writes the help screen for you. For testing, pass a list of strings to parse args instead of reading the real command line. If the input is invalid, argparse prints an error and exits.

slides.title: Command-line filters
slides.task:
Write `build_parser()` returning an `ArgumentParser` with:
- `--region`: text, default `None` (all regions)
- `--month`: text like `2026-02`, default `None`
- `--top`: an **int**, default `3`

Then `apply_filters(rows, args)`: keep rows matching the given region (ignoring case) and month.
slides.starter:
import argparse

rows = [
    {"month": "2026-01", "region": "North", "product": "Earbuds", "revenue": 4497.0},
    {"month": "2026-02", "region": "West", "product": "Phone case", "revenue": 1794.0},
    {"month": "2026-02", "region": "North", "product": "Smartwatch", "revenue": 9998.0},
    {"month": "2026-03", "region": "West", "product": "Charger", "revenue": 2397.0},
]

def build_parser():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Sales dashboard")
    # add --region, --month and --top here
    return parser

def apply_filters(rows, args):
    return rows

args = build_parser().parse_args([])    # then try ["--region", "West", "--top", "5"]
print(args)
print(apply_filters(rows, args))
slides.solution:
import argparse

rows = [
    {"month": "2026-01", "region": "North", "product": "Earbuds", "revenue": 4497.0},
    {"month": "2026-02", "region": "West", "product": "Phone case", "revenue": 1794.0},
    {"month": "2026-02", "region": "North", "product": "Smartwatch", "revenue": 9998.0},
    {"month": "2026-03", "region": "West", "product": "Charger", "revenue": 2397.0},
]

def build_parser():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Sales dashboard")
    parser.add_argument("--region", help="only this region, e.g. West")
    parser.add_argument("--month", help="only this month, e.g. 2026-02")
    parser.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=3, help="how many top products")
    return parser

def apply_filters(rows, args):
    return [r for r in rows
            if (args.region is None or r["region"].lower() == args.region.lower())
            and (args.month is None or r["month"] == args.month)]

args = build_parser().parse_args(["--region", "West", "--top", "5"])
print(args)
print(apply_filters(rows, args))
slides.tests:
p = build_parser()
a = p.parse_args([])
assert all(hasattr(a, name) for name in ("region", "month", "top")), "The parser needs three options, --region, --month and --top: add each with parser.add_argument."
assert a.region is None and a.month is None, "With no options, region and month should default to None, meaning everything."
assert a.top == 3, f"--top should default to 3, not {a.top!r}."
a = p.parse_args(["--top", "5"])
assert a.top == 5 and isinstance(a.top, int), "--top 5 should give the int 5: use type=int."
got = apply_filters(rows, p.parse_args(["--region", "West"]))
assert [r["product"] for r in got] == ["Phone case", "Charger"], f"--region West should keep the 2 West rows. Got {got}."
got = apply_filters(rows, p.parse_args(["--region", "north", "--month", "2026-02"]))
assert [r["product"] for r in got] == ["Smartwatch"], f"--region north --month 2026-02 should keep only North's February row (ignore case). Got {got}."
assert apply_filters(rows, p.parse_args([])) == rows, "With no filters, keep every row."
assert apply_filters([], p.parse_args(["--region", "East"])) == [], "Filtering no rows gives no rows."
hints: `parser.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=3)`. Options you don't give a default to are None.
Keep a row if `args.region is None` or the regions match: compare both with `.lower()`.
Join the region and month conditions with `and` inside a list comprehension.
slides.say: Real tools take options on the command line, like dash dash region West, dash dash top five. Build the parser with argparse: region and month are optional text, and top is a whole number that defaults to three. Then write apply filters to keep only the matching rows. Passing a list to parse args lets us test it without a terminal.

slides.title: Month-over-month growth
slides.task:
Write `growth(by_month)`: given `{month: revenue}`, return `(month, percent)` pairs in month order, where `percent` is the change from the previous month, rounded to 1 decimal.

The first month, and any month after a ₹0 month, gets `None`.
slides.starter:
def growth(by_month):
    result = []
    # sort the months, then compare each one with the month before
    return result

print(growth({"2026-02": 33000, "2026-01": 30000, "2026-03": 29700}))
# [('2026-01', None), ('2026-02', 10.0), ('2026-03', -10.0)]
slides.solution:
def growth(by_month):
    result, previous = [], None
    for month in sorted(by_month):
        revenue = by_month[month]
        if not previous:          # the first month, or the previous one was 0
            result.append((month, None))
        else:
            result.append((month, round((revenue - previous) / previous * 100, 1)))
        previous = revenue
    return result

print(growth({"2026-02": 33000, "2026-01": 30000, "2026-03": 29700}))
# [('2026-01', None), ('2026-02', 10.0), ('2026-03', -10.0)]
slides.tests:
got = growth({"2026-02": 33000, "2026-01": 30000, "2026-03": 29700})
assert got == [("2026-01", None), ("2026-02", 10.0), ("2026-03", -10.0)], f"Expected [('2026-01', None), ('2026-02', 10.0), ('2026-03', -10.0)], got {got}. Sort the months first."
assert growth({}) == [], "No months means an empty list."
assert growth({"2026-05": 1000}) == [("2026-05", None)], "A single month has nothing to compare with: None."
got = growth({"2026-01": 0, "2026-02": 500, "2026-03": 750})
assert got == [("2026-01", None), ("2026-02", None), ("2026-03", 50.0)], f"After a ₹0 month you can't divide by zero, so use None. Got {got}."
assert growth({"2026-01": 300, "2026-02": 400})[1][1] == 33.3, "300 to 400 is +33.3% when rounded to 1 decimal."
hints: Loop over `sorted(by_month)`: 'YYYY-MM' strings sort in date order.
Keep the previous month's revenue in a variable; `if not previous:` covers both None and 0.
slides.say: Managers love growth numbers. Write growth: for each month, in order, work out the percentage change from the month before, rounded to one decimal place. The first month has nothing to compare with, and you can never divide by a zero month, so both get None. Year and month strings sort correctly as plain text.
